study.title: Isaiah 2 The Mount of the LORD, the human pride, and the call to trust in God
study.overview: Isaiah 2 presents a strong contrast between the glorious future of God's rule and the present reality of pride, idolatry and human trust. In the first verses, the vision points to a time when the nations will run to Zion to learn the ways of the Lord, and peace will replace war. Then the prophet denounces Judah for adopting strange customs, amassing riches, relying on military forces and leaning before idols made by human hands. The message culminates in the day when the majesty of the Lord will humble all that man exalts, will dismantle all false security and make it impossible to sustain trust in human beings as the ultimate foundation.

outline.title: Zion's vision exalted and the peace of the nations
outline.explanation: Isaiah announces that in the last days the mountain of the house of the LORD will be raised above all and draw peoples of many nations. They will not come to conquer, but to learn the will of God and walk in their ways. The result of this divine teaching will be justice between nations and the end of the logic of war, with weapons transformed into instruments of life. The passage ends with a call right to the house of Jacob to walk in the light of the LORD.

outline.title: The guilt of Judah: strange customs, wealth, power, and idolatry
outline.explanation: The prophet moves from the future vision to the concrete condition of his people. Judah is taken by foreign practices, alliances with pagan peoples, material abundance and trust in horses and chariots, that is, in military power. The most serious sin is idolatry: the earth is full of images before which the people bow. Therefore, humiliation and lack of forgiveness appear as consequences of God's withdrawal.

outline.title: The Day of the Lord against all human pride
outline.explanation: The commandment to hide in the rocks shows the dread before the glorious presence of the LORD. The focus of judgment is pride: hive eyes, human greatness and everything that rises as a symbol of autonomy and power will be slaughtered. The list of cedars, oaks, hills, towers, walls, ships and desirable works represents the strength, wealth and human culture, all unable to resist divine judgment. The central point is repeated: only the Lord will be exalted.

outline.title: Fall of idols and final warning against trusting man
outline.explanation: When the LORD rises, idols disappear completely. What the people have made to worship will be cast out with contempt, as something unworthy and powerless. The final scene extends the dread: men and their false security guards hide because they do not bear divine glory. The chapter ends with a direct and practical appeal: to stop trusting in man, whose life is fragile and passing.

study.context: Chapter 2 functions as the beginning of a new prophetic discourse, linked to Judah and Jerusalem. The text alternates hope and denunciation: first, the future attraction of the nations to the mount of the LORD; then, the accusation against the present sinful of Judah. The notes highlight that the term Last days" points to the future, and that the prophet uses images of human structures - religious, military and social - to show that all this will be subjected to God's judgment.
study.theology: Chapter theology is centered on God's sovereignty over history. He is the teacher of the nations, the judge who corrects, the LORD whose glory fills the future and whose judgment overthrows every human pretense. There is also a strong criticism of idolatry and self-reliance: everything that replaces God's wealth, military power, human alliances, hand-made images is unstable and will be removed. In contrast, God's ideal for his people is to walk in his light, to live under his instruction and to anticipate a reconciled world, marked by peace and justice. For a Protestant evangelical reading, the text points to the reign of God that brings together peoples and unmasks false human security, without allowing man to occupy the place that belongs to the Lord.

scholarViews.insight: The section 2:5-22 shows that the prophecy of judgment confronts human pride in all areas of life, and verse 22 summarizes the contrast between trusting in the Lord and relying on man, whose strength is only temporary and fragile.
The chapter begins with the vision of the last days, understood as the era of the Messiah, when the nations would be drawn to Zion to learn the will of God and live in peace.
Verse 22 closes the call not to trust man or the gods invented by him, because none of them can save or destroy.

questions: In which areas of life do I trust more human resources than in the direction of the Lord?
What signs of pride, wealth or self-preservation may be competing with true worship in my heart?
How should the hope of a world governed by God shape my practice of peace, justice and discipleship today?
study.practice: Read this chapter as a spiritual examination. Reflect on which "horses," "cars" and "dollars" modern support their security: status, money, influence, knowledge, control or approval. Then, respond with concrete actions: confess your dependence on these things, reorganize priorities to seek God's instruction and practice an attitude of peace, not competition. The chapter also calls the community of faith to be a people who walk in the light of the Lord and witness to a different kingdom, in which glory belongs only to God.
study.uncertainty: The text provided brings some translated forms unusually and does not allow you to confirm certain details of the translation without resorting to other sources. It is also not possible to determine historically accurately, only on the basis of the notes provided, the final fulfillment of all images of the chapter; therefore, the reading of the messianic future and judgment is presented as interpretation supported by the notes, not as a single and incontroversial explanation.
